etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English honourable, from Old French honorable, honurable, from Latin honōrābilis, from honōrō (“I honour”); cognate with Italian onorabile, Spanish honorable. By surface analysis, honor +‎ -able. In this sense, largely displaced Old English ārfæst.

definitions.definition: Behaving in a manner that shows honor; decent, having integrity.

quote.citation: 1887, The Popular Science Monthly, volume 31, page 629:
quote.text: In confinement ladies are attended, not by the ordinary doctors, but by women especially devoted to the calling, who regard their profession as honorable and humanitary.

definitions.definition: Complying with cultural rules regarding honor; not provoking shame or disgrace.

quote.text: Luxury was abolished. People lived in honorable marriage. All the women were chaste, faithful, and far from wantoners.

definitions.definition: (politics) A courtesy title, given in Britain and the Commonwealth to a cabinet minister, minister of state, or senator, and in the United States to the president, vice president, congresspeople, state governors and legislators, and mayors.

quote.citation: 1872, Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, The Unkind Word, and Other Stories, page 145:
quote.text: Uncheered by friends, unhissed by foes, the honorable member blandly continued his speech  […]

definitions.definition: A politician or other person who bears the title of "honorable".

quote.citation: 1959, American Journal of Psychotherapy, volume 13, page 111:
quote.text: These included a reception for the Congress participants, given by the city of Barcelona in a 14th century palace, with guards making room for the mayor and other honorables,  […]
